title: 45 Hotel Logos Explained
author: Arek Dvornechuck

seo.title: 45 Hotel Logos Explained
seo.description: 45 hotel logos explained by a brand designer: global chains like Marriott and Hilton, luxury and 5-star brands like Four Seasons and Aman, boutique hotels, and iconic resorts.

description: 45 hotel logos explained by a brand designer: global chains like Marriott and Hilton, luxury and 5-star brands like Four Seasons and Aman, boutique hotels, and iconic resorts.
intro:
A hotel logo appears on the building, the key card, the bathrobe, the booking app, and the bill, so it has to feel welcoming, trustworthy, and a little aspirational. The best hotel logos signal the price point in a split second, from a friendly chain to a 5-star luxury brand.

What makes a good hotel logo?

The right level of formality: budget and midscale chains use bold, friendly type that reads from the highway, while luxury hotels use thin serifs, crests, and lots of white space.

A symbol that works small: a monogram, crest, or emblem has to work on a key card, a pillow, and an app icon, like the Hilton H, the Ritz-Carlton lion, or the Mandarin Oriental fan.

A story of place or heritage: many hotel logos borrow from their origins, like the traveller's palm of Raffles in Singapore or the Four Seasons tree.

Below are 45 hotel logos in five groups: global hotel groups, luxury hotel brands, upscale brands, lifestyle and boutique hotels, and resorts and iconic hotels. Each logo has a slide with my handwritten notes and a short explanation. If you are building a premium hospitality brand, see how I approach luxury branding, and read my guides to monogram logos, wordmark logos, and the branding process.

logoResearch.name: Marriott
logoResearch.verifiedFact: J. Willard and Alice Marriott started with a root beer stand in Washington, D.C., in 1927 and opened their first hotel in 1957.
observations: The flowing red script makes the world's largest hotel company feel personal, like a signature.
A small line underneath spells out "hotels, resorts, suites", so the script can stay large and expressive.

logoResearch.name: Hilton
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Conrad Hilton bought his first hotel, the Mobley in Cisco, Texas, in 1919.
observations: An H monogram in a circle works as an app icon and on signage, while the serif name carries the heritage.
Deep Hilton blue keeps the brand calm and trustworthy across thousands of properties.

logoResearch.name: Hyatt
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Hyatt began in 1957, when Jay Pritzker bought the Hyatt House motel next to Los Angeles International Airport.
observations: Thin, widely spaced capitals give the name a light, modern feel.
A blue arc sweeps under the letters like a smile, adding warmth to an otherwise strict wordmark.

logoResearch.name: IHG Hotels & Resorts
logoResearch.verifiedFact: IHG became an independent company in 2003 and adopted the "IHG Hotels & Resorts" name and logo in 2021.
observations: Three bold initials sit next to a two-line descriptor, so the group name is clear without a symbol.
The all-black logo lets the colourful brands it owns, like Holiday Inn and InterContinental, take the spotlight.

logoResearch.name: Accor
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Paul Dubrule and Gérard Pélisson opened the first Novotel near Lille in 1967, and the group returned to the simple Accor name in 2019.
observations: A gold A, shaped like a stylized peak, gives the group a luxurious symbol.
Spaced capitals underneath keep the wordmark quiet and premium.

logoResearch.name: Wyndham
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Wyndham was founded in Dallas in 1981 by real estate developer Trammell Crow.
observations: Wide blue capitals make the name easy to read on highway signs and building tops.
A thin swoosh and a small descriptor line underneath add movement and context.

logoResearch.name: Radisson
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The first Radisson Hotel opened in Minneapolis in 1909, named after French explorer Pierre-Esprit Radisson.
observations: The bold brush script feels energetic and hospitable, unlike the strict type of most chains.
A teal underline finishes the script and adds a fresh accent colour.

logoResearch.name: Best Western
logoResearch.verifiedFact: M.K. Guertin founded Best Western in 1946 as a referral network of independent hotels.
observations: The BW initials work as a compact mark, separated from the name by a thin line.
Rounded, friendly letters in deep blue make the brand feel approachable and reliable.

logoResearch.name: Holiday Inn
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Kemmons Wilson opened the first Holiday Inn in Memphis, Tennessee, in 1952.
observations: The green script H recalls the brand's famous "Great Sign" from the 1950s and 60s roadside motels.
The friendly italic wordmark and small "by IHG" line connect the brand to its parent company.

logoResearch.name: The Ritz-Carlton
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The brand takes its name from Swiss hotelier César Ritz, and The Ritz-Carlton Boston, opened in 1927, set the standard for the modern brand.
observations: The lion and crown emblem gives the brand an aristocratic, almost heraldic feel.
Serif capitals joined by a hyphen keep the name formal and elegant.

logoResearch.name: Four Seasons
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Isadore Sharp opened the first Four Seasons, a motor hotel in Toronto, in 1961.
observations: The tree symbol represents the four seasons, with leaves that suggest growth and nature.
The small caps wordmark under the tree is quiet and refined, typical of luxury hotels.

logoResearch.name: St. Regis
logoResearch.verifiedFact: John Jacob Astor IV opened The St. Regis New York in 1904.
observations: The ornate monogram looks like a family crest, a nod to the Astor heritage.
Widely spaced capitals next to it keep the logo balanced and formal.

logoResearch.name: Waldorf Astoria
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The Waldorf Astoria New York opened on Park Avenue in 1931, replacing the original hotel from the 1890s.
observations: The interlocking WA monogram is inspired by the hotel's Art Deco heritage.
The two names stack in small, soft grey capitals, which keeps the logo understated.

logoResearch.name: Mandarin Oriental
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Mandarin Oriental grew from The Mandarin in Hong Kong, which opened in 1963.
observations: The gold fan is the brand's signature symbol, linking it to its Asian roots.
Each hotel in the group has its own version of the fan, which makes the symbol collectable.

logoResearch.name: The Peninsula
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The Peninsula Hong Kong opened in 1928, and it is the flagship of the Peninsula Hotels group.
observations: Classic serif capitals give the name the feel of a grand old hotel.
A thin rule and widely spaced "Hotels" underneath add a finishing, formal touch.

logoResearch.name: Rosewood
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Caroline Rose Hunt founded Rosewood in Dallas in 1979 with The Mansion on Turtle Creek.
observations: Wide, heavy capitals with generous spacing give a short name a strong presence.
With no symbol, the wordmark relies entirely on proportion and spacing.

logoResearch.name: Aman
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Adrian Zecha opened the first Aman, Amanpuri in Phuket, in 1988, and aman means "peace" in Sanskrit.
observations: The A's are drawn without crossbars, so the letters feel open and calm.
A small macron over the first A adds a subtle, almost spiritual detail.

logoResearch.name: Belmond
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Orient-Express Hotels was renamed Belmond in 2014, and LVMH acquired the group in 2019.
observations: Spaced geometric capitals look modern while still feeling refined.
The single-word name replaced the old Orient-Express branding, which belonged to a different train company.

logoResearch.name: Sheraton
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Ernest Henderson and Robert Moore founded Sheraton in 1937 in Springfield, Massachusetts.
observations: The S inside a laurel wreath looks like a seal of quality.
The brand name famously came from an illuminated hotel sign that was too expensive to replace.

logoResearch.name: Westin
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Westin began as Western Hotels in Seattle in 1930, and the Westin name was adopted later.
observations: Heavy, high-contrast serif letters give the name a confident, classic look.
A warm bronze colour and spaced descriptor underneath feel calm and premium.

logoResearch.name: InterContinental
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Pan American World Airways founded InterContinental Hotels in 1946 to house travellers on its new routes.
observations: A gold I inside a medallion acts like a coin or a seal.
The serif capitals with a small dot recall the golden age of international air travel.

logoResearch.name: Conrad
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Hilton launched Conrad as its luxury brand in 1982, naming it after founder Conrad Hilton.
observations: The A without a crossbar gives the gold capitals a distinctive, modern twist.
The brand uses the founder's first name, which makes it feel personal and exclusive.

logoResearch.name: Fairmont
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The Fairmont San Francisco opened in 1907, and the brand is now part of Accor.
observations: The large flourished F turns the wordmark into an elegant signature.
The calligraphic script suggests old-world hospitality and grand hotels.

logoResearch.name: Kempinski
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Kempinski is Europe's oldest luxury hotel group, with roots in Berthold Kempinski's business in Berlin.
observations: The flowing signature script looks like a handwritten name, which feels personal.
The "Hoteliers since 1897" line underneath stresses the brand's long heritage.

logoResearch.name: Shangri-La
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Robert Kuok opened the first Shangri-La hotel in Singapore in 1971, naming it after the paradise in the novel Lost Horizon.
observations: The gold S symbol looks like mountains reflected in water, a nod to the mythical place.
Spaced capitals and a small descriptor underneath keep the logo balanced and formal.

logoResearch.name: Sofitel
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Accor's founders opened the first Sofitel in Strasbourg, France, in 1964.
observations: Extremely wide letter spacing gives the short name an airy, elegant feel.
Geometric capitals keep the logo modern and very French.

logoResearch.name: Grand Hyatt
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The first Grand Hyatt opened in New York in 1980, next to Grand Central Terminal.
observations: White capitals inside a red bar make the logo look like a bold sign.
A thin vertical line separates the two words, so each one reads clearly.

logoResearch.name: W Hotels
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The first W Hotel opened in New York in 1998.
observations: A single letter W is all the brand needs, which makes it feel confident and design-led.
The tiny descriptor underneath almost disappears, so the W does all the work.

logoResearch.name: Ace Hotel
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Alex Calderwood, Wade Weigel and Doug Herrick opened the first Ace Hotel in Seattle in 1999.
observations: Condensed capitals in a heavy black frame look like a vintage hotel sign.
The logo feels more like a record label than a hotel brand, which fits its creative audience.

logoResearch.name: Edition
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Edition is a partnership between Marriott and hotelier Ian Schrager, who co-founded Studio 54.
observations: High-contrast serif capitals look like a fashion magazine masthead.
A line cutting through the O adds one unexpected detail to an otherwise classic wordmark.

logoResearch.name: 1 Hotels
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Barry Sternlicht launched 1 Hotels, opening the first one in Miami Beach in 2015.
observations: A giant serif 1 dominates the logo, so the brand name is a single character.
A deep green colour reflects the brand's focus on nature and sustainability.

logoResearch.name: Kimpton
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Bill Kimpton opened his first boutique hotel in San Francisco in 1981.
observations: A clean sans serif wordmark keeps the founder's name simple and friendly.
The minimal logo lets each Kimpton hotel have its own personality and design.

logoResearch.name: Hotel Indigo
logoResearch.verifiedFact: IHG launched Hotel Indigo in 2004, with the first hotel in Atlanta.
observations: The two words stack, with a large INDIGO under a smaller HOTEL.
The deep indigo blue matches the brand name, which makes it easy to remember.

logoResearch.name: The Hoxton
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The first Hoxton hotel opened in Shoreditch, London, in 2006.
observations: Bold lowercase letters make the name feel relaxed and approachable.
The heavy, slightly quirky serif gives the brand a neighbourhood pub feel.

logoResearch.name: citizenM
logoResearch.verifiedFact: citizenM opened its first hotel at Amsterdam Schiphol Airport in 2008.
observations: A bold red M symbol works as an icon, while "citizen" sits above in lowercase.
The playful lowercase name signals the brand's casual, tech-friendly style.

logoResearch.name: Moxy
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Marriott launched Moxy in 2014, with the first hotel at Milan Malpensa Airport.
observations: Loopy, handwritten letters make the logo feel playful and young.
Bright magenta is unusual for a hotel brand, and it stands out instantly.

logoResearch.name: Six Senses
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Sonu and Eva Shivdasani founded Six Senses in 1995, and IHG bought the brand in 2019.
observations: A small pattern of dots sits above the name, like stones or seeds.
Thin, widely spaced capitals make the wellness brand feel calm and quiet.

logoResearch.name: One&Only
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Kerzner International launched One&Only as its ultra-luxury resort brand in 2002.
observations: The flowing italic script makes the name feel romantic and exclusive.
The ampersand joins the two words into one continuous signature.

logoResearch.name: Banyan Tree
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Ho Kwon Ping and Claire Chiang opened the first Banyan Tree resort in Phuket, Thailand, in 1994.
observations: The banyan tree illustration has trunks that look like figures, which suggests shelter and community.
Hand-drawn capitals underneath feel natural and handcrafted.

logoResearch.name: Club Med
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Gérard Blitz founded Club Med in 1950, and its trident symbol dates back to the brand's early years.
observations: Bold, rounded blue letters feel friendly and holiday-ready.
The trident next to the name is a nod to the sea and the brand's beach villages.

logoResearch.name: Atlantis
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Sol Kerzner opened Atlantis Paradise Island in the Bahamas in the 1990s.
observations: Wide, spaced capitals in ocean blue make the name feel grand and aquatic.
The location line underneath connects the brand to its flagship resort.

logoResearch.name: Raffles
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Raffles Hotel Singapore opened in 1887, named after Sir Stamford Raffles.
observations: The traveller's palm illustration links the brand to its tropical Singapore origins.
Bold, spaced capitals underneath balance the detailed drawing.

logoResearch.name: The Savoy
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Richard D'Oyly Carte opened the Savoy in London in 1889.
observations: Thin, elegant capitals make the short name look refined and timeless.
Wide spacing gives each letter room, like the hotel's famous Art Deco interiors.

logoResearch.name: The Plaza
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The Plaza opened at Fifth Avenue and Central Park South in New York in 1907.
observations: A gold crest above the name gives the hotel a regal, monumental feel.
Classic serif capitals and a small "New York" line underneath tie the brand to its city.

logoResearch.name: Jumeirah
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Jumeirah was founded in Dubai in 1997, and its Burj Al Arab hotel opened in 1999.
observations: Elegant serif capitals keep the logo calm, even though the brand's hotels are spectacular.
The long J extends below the line, giving the name a distinctive first letter.

listIntro: The boards below show all 45 hotel logos in one consistent format, grouped into global groups, luxury brands, upscale brands, lifestyle and boutique hotels, and resorts and iconic hotels.
Each logo is reviewed for its design decisions, not for the hotels' size, service, or star rating.
sectionIntroductions: The biggest hotel companies need logos that work on thousands of buildings, highway signs, and loyalty apps, so they favour bold type and strong colour.
Luxury and 5-star hotel brands rely on crests, monograms, and refined serifs that feel like a private club.
Upscale brands sit between the chains and the palaces, mixing classic serifs and scripts with a signature colour.
Lifestyle and boutique hotels behave more like fashion or music brands, with playful type, single letters, and bold colour.
Resorts and iconic hotels borrow from their place: palms, trees, tridents, crests, and the cities they made famous.
sectionBridge: This is a visual comparison of hotel logos, not a ranking of hotels.
Look at how each logo uses type, a symbol, or colour to signal its price point and personality.
entryFallbacks: The identity relies on a few clear decisions to stay recognizable.
Notice how the logo would look on a key card, a building sign, and a booking app.

findings.heading: Luxury hotels whisper, chains shout
findings.text: Four Seasons, Aman, Rosewood, and The Savoy use thin, spaced type and quiet colours, while Holiday Inn, Best Western, and Wyndham use bold, friendly letters that read from the road.

findings.heading: Crests and monograms signal heritage
findings.text: The Ritz-Carlton lion, the St. Regis monogram, the Waldorf Astoria WA, and the Plaza crest borrow from heraldry to suggest a long, aristocratic history.

findings.heading: Boutique hotels think like fashion brands
findings.text: W Hotels, Edition, Ace Hotel, and citizenM use single letters, magazine-style serifs, sign-like frames, and bold colour to attract a design-minded audience.

findings.heading: Place is a powerful idea
findings.text: Raffles' traveller's palm, the Banyan Tree illustration, the Club Med trident, and the Shangri-La mountain all tie the brand to a destination.

logoRosterConfig.checklistHeading: A practical checklist for a hotel logo
checklistItems: Does the logo signal the right price point, from friendly midscale to 5-star luxury?
Does it work on a building sign, a key card, a robe, and an app icon?
Is there a monogram or symbol that can stand alone on amenities and small items?
Does it reflect the place, heritage, or personality of the hotel?
Will it still look right when printed in one colour, embossed, or embroidered?

faq.question: What makes a good hotel logo?
faq.answer: A good hotel logo signals the right price point, works on everything from building signs to key cards and apps, and has a memorable symbol or wordmark. Luxury hotels usually use refined serifs and crests, while midscale chains use bold, friendly type.

faq.question: What do 5-star hotel logos have in common?
faq.answer: Most 5-star and luxury hotel logos use thin serif or widely spaced capitals, lots of white space, and a crest, monogram, or emblem, like The Ritz-Carlton lion, the Four Seasons tree, or the Mandarin Oriental fan. Colour is usually limited to black, gold, or one muted tone.

faq.question: Should a hotel logo have a symbol?
faq.answer: A symbol helps when the logo needs to appear on small items like key cards, pillows, toiletries, and app icons. Many hotels pair a full wordmark with a monogram or emblem that can stand on its own, like Hilton, Sheraton, and St. Regis.

faq.question: What colours do hotel logos use?
faq.answer: Luxury hotels favour black, gold, and soft neutrals, while big chains use strong blues, greens, and reds that stand out on signs and in booking apps. Lifestyle brands like Moxy and citizenM use bolder colours to look young and energetic.

faq.question: How much does a hotel logo cost?
faq.answer: A professional hotel logo and brand identity from an experienced designer usually costs from a few thousand dollars for a small boutique hotel to much more for a full hospitality brand system with signage and amenities. The final cost depends on the scope, the number of applications, and the research involved.
